title: Degreasing without damage
audience: Cleaners doing kitchen, appliance and splashback degreasing in residential, commercial, bond and short-stay settings.
learningOutcomes: Distinguish loose food residue, light oil films, hardened grease and mineral deposits.
Select an approved degreasing method that suits the surface.
Degrease a surface in a controlled sequence without damaging its finish.

instruction.heading: Identify the soil and the surface
instruction.body: Grease is not one thing. A light oil film on stainless steel behaves differently from hardened grease on an oven shelf or a baked-on residue on a painted panel. Loose crumbs and food residue come off with dry methods first. Before applying a degreaser, identify the surface: stainless steel, laminate, painted surfaces, glass, coated metal, sealed stone and timber all respond differently. Damaged coatings and porous surfaces may need specialist advice rather than a stronger product.

instruction.heading: Choose an approved method
instruction.body: Read the product label and SDS for the intended surface, dilution, PPE, ventilation, dwell time and rinsing. Check the appliance or benchtop manufacturer's guidance where it is available. Avoid aggressive abrasives on polished stainless steel and coated surfaces, because they leave scratches that hold more grease later. Avoid acidic or strongly alkaline products on sensitive stone, timber or finishes unless the product is approved for that surface.

instruction.heading: Degrease in a controlled sequence
instruction.body: Remove loose debris first so that it does not smear. Apply the authorised product using the label method and wait for the specified time without letting the product dry where the label prohibits that. Agitate with a compatible non-scratching tool, lift the residue, rinse if the label directs, and dry the surface where appropriate. Keep drips away from food, power sockets and appliance controls. Degreasing near electrical controls needs extra care, and the product must not be allowed to enter switches or vents.

instruction.heading: Checking the result and escalating
instruction.body: Inspect the surface from more than one angle, because streaks and residue often show only in side light. Repeat the method only within the approved method. Record baked-on or inaccessible grease as a limitation rather than increasing the chemical strength without approval. Where a surface is damaged by the process, stop, record the damage, and report it. Do not hide the damage by applying another product.

procedure: Identify the soil type and the surface material before choosing a method.
Read the label and SDS for surface, dilution, PPE, ventilation, dwell time and rinsing.
Remove loose debris first, then apply the authorised product using the label method.
Agitate with a compatible non-scratching tool, lift the residue, rinse and dry as directed.
Protect food, sockets and appliance controls from drips throughout.
Inspect the surface from several angles, and record limitations or damage.

workedExamples.situation: A cleaner is asked to scrub a brushed stainless-steel splashback with a harsh abrasive pad.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What method do you choose, and what do you record?
workedExamples.reasoning: Use a compatible non-scratching method approved for stainless steel, and test first only if the procedure allows. Abrasive scrubbing scratches the brushed finish and traps more grease, so do not use it. Record any remaining grease as a limitation and any existing damage separately.

equipmentAndPpe: Approved degreaser with label and SDS available.
Gloves and eye protection as set by the SDS.
Drip protection for food, sockets and controls.

commonErrors.error: Using a harsh abrasive on polished stainless steel.
commonErrors.prevention: Use a compatible non-scratching method and check the surface first.

commonErrors.error: Letting degreaser dry on the surface when the label prohibits it.
commonErrors.prevention: Follow the label dwell and rinsing rules.

commonErrors.error: Increasing product strength to remove baked-on grease without approval.
commonErrors.prevention: Record the limitation and escalate for an approved method.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Degreasers are chemicals. The label and SDS govern PPE, ventilation and disposal, and the workplace hazardous chemicals register applies where one is kept.

qualityStandard: Correct method chosen for four mock surfaces and three soil types.
One grease-removal sequence completed without damage to the finish.
Limitations recorded for any residue that could not be removed by the approved method.
documentationEvidence: Method and product record for the job.
Limitation or damage record with photos where permitted.
summary: Identify the soil and the surface before choosing a product.
Use the label method, non-scratching tools and controlled rinsing.
Protect food and controls from drips.
Record limitations and damage rather than escalating product strength.

knowledgeChecks.question: Why is an abrasive pad a poor choice on polished stainless steel?
options: It makes the surface shine more and it hides grime for a while
It removes the product label and any approved instructions
It scratches the finish, and scratches can trap more grease later

knowledgeChecks.question: Baked-on grease remains after the approved method. What do you do?
options: Record the limitation and escalate for an approved method
Use a stronger product without asking if the stain is old
Leave the item and say nothing to the client or the team

knowledgeChecks.question: What must you protect during degreasing?
options: The client's car, the garden hose and the parked bicycle
Food, power sockets and appliance controls from drips
The floor and the skirting boards, which are the main risk
